source.title: LIMI: Less is More for Agency
source.authors: Yang Xiao; Mo-Han Jiang; Jie Sun; Ke-Yu Li; Ji-Fan Lin; Yumin Zhuang; Ji Zeng; Shi-Jie Xia; Qishuo Hua; Xue-Feng Li; Xiao-Jie Cai; Tong Wang; Yue Zhang; Li-Ming Liu; Xia Wu; Jin-Long Hou; Yuan Cheng; Wenjie Li; Xiang Wang; De-Quan Wang; Peng-Fei Liu

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses and challenges the broad assumption that more training data improves agentic capability, but it does not test pretraining-loss scaling laws, their extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation. Its results concern agency-focused fine-tuning, not the claim versions’ pretraining-loss behavior.
record.gate_note: The paper reports agent-benchmark results after fine-tuning on datasets with different sizes, but those experiments do not measure held-out pretraining loss or test a version of the claim. Fine-tuning is deliberately directed at agentic behavior, so the results do not establish how that behavior arises without the inducement. Reported numerical comparisons are recorded as adjacent findings under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper fine-tunes GLM-4.5 and GLM-4.5-Air on small curated agentic datasets and compares agency-benchmark scores against fine-tuning on other, larger datasets. It invokes Kaplan et al. rhetorically as the 'more data' paradigm it rejects, but it measures no pretraining loss and runs no scaling sweep. It fits no power law and makes no downstream-predictability test: the datasets differ in content, not just size. Its results do not bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that agency emerges from strategic curation of a few high-quality demonstrations rather than data abundance (the 'Agency Efficiency Principle'). They frame this as challenging conventional scaling paradigms in agentic AI development, specifically fine-tuning data scaling, not pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes models on agentic demonstrations and evaluates agency benchmarks; it does not reproduce pretraining-loss scaling measurements or compute-allocation fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper compares different training datasets and curation strategies, so outcomes vary with dataset choice as well as sample count.

fits_no_version.finding: On AgencyBench, GLM-4.5 fine-tuned on 78 curated samples scored 73.5. Fine-tuning on other agentic datasets of 260, 7,610 and 10,000 samples scored 29.2, 36.7 and 47.8 (Table 2). The datasets differ in content and curation, and no uncertainty is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In agentic SFT, data curation and quality can outweigh sample count; small curated sets beat larger uncontrolled alternatives.

record.problems: The data-efficiency comparison changes dataset content and curation along with sample count, so it does not isolate a sample-volume effect. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these scores and provides no controlled pretraining scaling sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version result rows were identified. Other reported benchmark scores and model comparisons were omitted because they do not measure any listed claim version.

untested.parts: Power-law pretraining loss in parameters, tokens or compute
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count
Power laws in other modalities or in fine-tuning; no controlled fine-tuning data-size sweep
Downstream predictability from scale or loss. The 106B vs 355B comparison is two points with different base models, and no fit is made.
Fit-dependence of exponents or compute-optimal split

record.verdict_notes: The reference to scaling laws (Kaplan et al.) is rhetorical framing only. The comparison confounds data content with size, so it says nothing about power-law behaviour of fine-tuning data. The Table 3 averages include AgencyBench scores. There is a URL error for the CodeAgent dataset (footnote 8).

versions.untested_parts: Power-law held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation trends.
Effects of architecture details such as depth and width at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; the reported downstream evaluations follow agency-focused fine-tuning and do not test such predictability.
Dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices.
